b: Estimate: probable cost of a work, calculated before construction.
Quantity surveying: working out quantities of items of work and their cost.
Bill of Quantities (BOQ): itemised list of quantities with rates; basis of tender.
Abstract of estimate: quantities × rates → cost of each item; totals.
Specification: describes quality of materials and workmanship (general / detailed).
Measurement sheet: records item, No., L, B, H/D, quantity.
Lump sum (L.S.): provision for items whose quantities cannot be worked out (e.g. electrification).
Contingencies: 3–5% of estimated cost, for unforeseen expenses.
Work-charged establishment: 1.5–2% (some departments up to 2.5%), staff paid from works.
Centage charges: 10–15% added for departmental establishment, T&P and design.
Prime cost (P.C.): cost of articles bought from market (fittings, sanitary ware).
Provisional sum: amount kept for work not fully defined at tender stage.
Day work: work paid on actual labour/material/time basis.
Preliminary / approximate / rough estimate: for administrative approval; based on cost of similar works.
Plinth area estimate: plinth area × plinth area rate. Plinth area = covered built-up area at floor level (outer dimensions of walls).
Cube rate estimate: plinth area × height × cube rate; height = floor top to roof top (more accurate than plinth area method for multi-storey).
Approximate quantity method: cost per running metre of wall (foundation + superstructure).
Detailed estimate: item-wise quantities × rates; for technical sanction and tender.
Revised estimate: when original sanctioned estimate is exceeded by more than 5% or design changes.
Supplementary estimate: for additional works found necessary during execution.
Annual repair / maintenance estimate: for upkeep of existing structure (≈1–1.5% of capital cost).
Complete estimate: total cost including land, roads, services, etc.
Per m² plinth area / per m³
Plinth area: built-up area at floor level incl. wall thickness (excludes open courtyards, cornices, chajjas).
Carpet area: usable area = plinth area − (walls, verandahs, corridors, stairs, kitchen, toilets…). ≈ 50–65% of plinth area (residential).
Circulation area: corridors, stairs, lobbies (≈10–20% of plinth area).
Built-up area: floor area + wall area (practically = plinth area).

Long wall – short wall method (out-to-out / in-to-in): long walls taken out-to-out, short walls in-to-in. Most accurate for unequal wall thickness.
Long wall L (c/c) = centre-to-centre length + one breadth.
Centre line method: total centre line length × breadth × height. Fast; best for walls of same section.
Correction in centre line method: deduct ½ × breadth × no. of T-junctions (for each junction) from total centre line length.
No deduction at corners (L-junctions) in centre line method.
Crossing / partly centre-line method: used where walls of different thickness meet.

b: Lead: horizontal distance for carrying excavated earth. Normal lead = 30 m (CPWD: 50 m).
Lift: vertical height through which earth is lifted. Normal lift = 1.5 m.
Extra lead/lift charged separately beyond normal values.
Initial lead and lift included in the rate of earthwork.
Foundation trench excavation = L × B × D (B = width of base concrete).
Shrinkage / settlement allowance in filling: 10% (consolidated filling deducted for voids).
Swell/bulking of earth after excavation: ordinary soil ≈ 10–25%, rock ≈ 40–60%.
Earthwork quantity in pits: 'dead man' (mud pillars) left to check depth; borrow pits used for embankment.
Cross-sectional area (level ground, bank): A = Bd + sd² (B = formation width, d = depth/height, s:1 = side slope H:V).
Mid-sectional area method: Q = L × A at mean depth (dm = (d1+d2)/2). Most commonly used.
Mean-sectional (average end area) method: Q = L × (A1 + A2)/2. Gives larger quantity; less accurate.
Trapezoidal formula: Q = d[(A1 + An)/2 + A2 + A3 + … + An−1].
Prismoidal formula (most accurate): Q = (d/3)[(A1 + An) + 4(even areas) + 2(remaining odd areas)]; needs odd number of sections.
Prismoidal correction: Cp = (L/6) × s × (d1 − d2)² (for level sections).
Curvature correction applied for earthwork on curves (Pappus's theorem).
Simpson's rule (areas): A = (d/3)[(O1+On) + 4ΣO_even + 2ΣO_odd]; requires odd no. of ordinates.

Rate analysis: determining rate per unit of an item = materials + labour + T&P + overheads + profit.
Purpose: fix contract rates, check contractor's rates, compare tenders, prepare estimates.
Factors: specifications, quantity/quality of materials, labour output, location, lead, season, profit.
Materials cost includes: cost at source + carriage + loading/unloading + storage + wastage.
Task / out-turn: work done by one labourer per day (e.g. mason brickwork ≈ 1.25 m³/day; earthwork ≈ 2.8–3 m³/day per labourer).
Schedule of rates (SOR / MRS / CSR): standard rates by PWD / department (Pakistan: Composite Schedule of Rates – CSR; Market Rate System – MRS).
Rate analysis normally done for 1 unit or a standard quantity (e.g. 10 m³ concrete, 100 m² plaster).
General (brief) specification: short description of type & quality; used in preliminary estimates.
Detailed specification: full description of materials, proportions, method of construction, curing, measurements; used in detailed estimate & contract.
Standard specification: published by departments (PWD, CPWD, BIS).
Writing order: same as sequence of construction (earthwork → foundation → DPC → superstructure → finishing).
In conflict: specification > drawings (generally detailed drawing > general drawing; written dims > scaled dims).
Tender: written offer by contractor to execute work at stated rates/amount, within time.
NIT (Notice Inviting Tender): advertisement of work, cost, earnest money, time, documents.
Earnest money (bid security): 1–2% of estimated cost (commonly 2%); refunded to unsuccessful bidders.
Security deposit (performance security): 5–10% of contract amount (commonly 10%, incl. earnest money); refunded after defect liability period.
Retention money: % deducted from each running bill (≈ 5–10%) until completion/defects liability.
Defect liability (maintenance) period: usually 6–12 months after completion.
Mobilization advance: ≈ 10% of contract value, recovered from bills.
Single tender, limited tender, open tender, global tender, two-envelope (technical + financial) tender.
Unbalanced tender: some item rates too high, others too low.
Lowest tender usually accepted (L1), subject to competence; tender committee evaluates.
Lump sum contract: fixed total amount for whole work; extra items paid as per schedule. Suitable where design is complete.
Item rate (unit price / schedule) contract: payment on measured quantities × quoted unit rates. Most common in PWD.
Percentage rate contract: contractor quotes % above/below the department's schedule of rates.
Cost plus percentage: actual cost + agreed % profit (no incentive to economise).
Cost plus fixed fee: actual cost + fixed fee.
Cost plus variable fee / target cost: fee varies with performance vs target.
Labour contract: department supplies materials; contractor supplies labour only.
Material supply contract: supply of materials only.
Turnkey (design & build / EPC): contractor responsible for design, construction, commissioning.
Piece-work agreement: small works, no tender, payment for completed work (limited amount).
Work order: written order for small works without formal contract.
Measurement Book (MB): official record of measurements; basis of all payments.
Running (on-account) bill: periodic payment for work done; final bill after completion.
Muster roll: record of daily labour attendance and wages.
Extra item: item not in original contract; Substituted item: replaces a contract item.
Deviation: variation in quantity beyond permitted limit (often ±10–20%).
Liquidated damages: penalty for delay (e.g. ≈ 0.5–1% per week, capped ≈ 10%).
Arbitration: settlement of disputes by arbitrator (Arbitration Act).
Force majeure: unforeseeable events (war, flood, earthquake) releasing liability.
Escalation clause: allows rate adjustment for price rise of materials/labour.
Imprest: advance cash to field officer for petty expenses.

Valuation: determining present fair value of a property.
Purposes: sale/purchase, mortgage/loan, taxation, rent fixation, insurance, compensation (acquisition), betterment levy.
Market value: price obtainable in open market at a given time (varies).
Book value: original cost − depreciation to date (as per account books).
Scrap value: value of dismantled materials (≈ 10% of cost for buildings).
Salvage value: value at end of useful life without dismantling (property used for other purposes).
Distress value: value under forced sale (lower than market value).
Speculative value: purchase with future gain in mind.
Potential value: value considering possible future development.
Accommodation value: extra value to a particular buyer.
Monopoly value: due to unique location/no competition.
Replacement value: cost of replacing existing property with similar one.
Reversionary value: value receivable after expiry of lease.
Gross income: total income from property; Net income = gross income − outgoings.
Outgoings: taxes, repairs (≈ 10–12% of gross rent), insurance, management, sinking fund, loss of rent.
Annuity: fixed annual payment for a fixed period.
Obsolescence: loss of value due to outdated design/technology (functional loss, not physical).
Freehold: absolute ownership; Leasehold: right to use for fixed period under lease.
Easement: right of a person over another's land (light, air, way).
Mortgage: transfer of interest in property as security for a loan.
Year's purchase (YP), perpetuity: YP = 100 / rate of interest (%) = 1/i.
YP for n years (single rate): YP = 1 / (i + is), where is = sinking fund coefficient.
Capitalised value = Net annual income × YP.
Annual sinking fund instalment: I = S × i / [(1 + i)ⁿ − 1], S = amount to be accumulated.
Present value of ₨1 due after n years: PV = 1 / (1 + i)ⁿ (deferred value).
Amount after n years (compound): A = P(1 + i)ⁿ.
Rent fixation: Rent = (interest on capital + sinking fund + outgoings) per year.
Straight line method: equal annual depreciation; D = (C − S)/n (C = cost, S = scrap, n = life).
Constant percentage / declining balance method: fixed % on reduced book value each year; D = 1 − (S/C)^(1/n). Never reaches zero.
Sinking fund method: annual amount set aside with compound interest to accumulate (C − S) at end of life.
Quantity survey method: depreciation based on assessed remaining life/condition.
Sum of years' digits method: higher depreciation in early years.
Life of buildings (approx.): RCC framed 75–100 yrs; load bearing brick 50–75 yrs; temporary 5–10 yrs.
Rental method: net income × YP (for rented properties).
Direct comparison with capital value: comparing recent sales of similar properties.
Valuation based on profit: hotels, cinemas, shops (net profit capitalised).
Development method: for land/building with development potential.
Depreciation method (cost method): present cost − depreciation (land value added).
Belting method: for land with road frontage; land divided in belts parallel to road. Belt depths ratio front:middle:rear values ≈ 100% : ⅔ (some texts ¾) : ½; front belt depth ≈ 15–25 m.
Land value usually determined by comparison; building value by depreciation.

Project – temporary endeavour with a definite start and end, producing a unique product, service or result
Operation – ongoing, repetitive work (opposite of a project)

Programme – group of related projects managed together; Portfolio – collection of projects/programmes to meet strategic goals

Cost and staffing – low at start, peak during execution, drop at closing

Horizontal bars – length of bar ∝ duration of activity; x-axis = time
Advantages – simple, easy to read, useful for progress monitoring
Limitations – does not show interdependency of activities, no critical path, no float, unsuitable for large projects
Milestone chart – improvement of bar chart; shows key events (milestones) on bars – still no interdependency
Activity – task consuming time and resources; shown by arrow (AOA)
Event (node) – instant of time; start or end of activity; consumes no time or resources
Dummy activity – zero time and zero resources; shown by dashed arrow; maintains logic / avoids two activities with same i-j
Merge event – two or more activities end at it; Burst event – two or more activities start from it
AOA (Activity on Arrow) – i-j method; used in CPM/PERT; may need dummies

Fulkerson's rule – method of numbering events (i < j for every activity)
Network rules – only one initial and one final event; no looping; no dangling activity; time flows left to right
Looping (cycling) – error – activity loops back to an earlier event
Dangling – error – activity not connected to final event
FS (Finish-to-Start) – most common; B starts after A finishes
Used for – repetitive works – highways, pipelines, housing units, tunnels, high-rise floors
Also called – linear scheduling method / vertical production method

Crashing – reducing project duration by adding resources to critical activities
Normal time / cost – duration at minimum direct cost
Crash time / cost – minimum possible duration at maximum direct cost
Cost slope – (Crash cost − Normal cost) / (Normal time − Crash time)
Rule – crash the critical activity with the LEAST cost slope first
Parallel critical paths – crash both paths simultaneously
Direct cost – labour, material, equipment – INCREASES as duration decreases

Law: Pakistan Engineering Council Act 1976 — PEC regulates engineering education and profession; CPD Bye-laws 2008 introduced the Professional Engineer (PE) route through the Engineering Practice Examination (EPE).

Registration: Graduate of a PEC-accredited programme → Registered Engineer (RE). Only registered engineers may perform professional engineering work; engineering firms are registered as consulting engineers or constructors/operators (categories C-A, C-B, C-1 … C-6).

Professional Engineer (PE): RE with ≥ 5 years of relevant experience after registration and ≥ 17 CPD points (10 from work experience + 7 from other CPD activities) may sit the EPE; passing gives the PE title. CPD points are also needed for renewal of registration.
International recognition: PEC is a full signatory of the Washington Accord (2017) — accredited Pakistani engineering degrees are recognised by other signatories.
Accreditation: Engineering Accreditation Board (EAB) of PEC accredits programmes on outcome-based education (OBE) — graduate attributes / programme learning outcomes.

Core ethical duties (PEC code & NSPE canons): Hold paramount public safety, health and welfare; work only within competence; be objective and truthful in reports and statements; act as faithful agent/trustee for employer or client; avoid and disclose conflicts of interest; no bribery or acceptance of commissions from contractors/suppliers; do not injure the reputation of other engineers or supplant them unfairly; sign and seal only work done under your own supervision; maintain confidentiality.
Whistle-blowing: If an employer overrules engineering judgment where life or property is endangered, the engineer must notify the client/competent authority.
PEC Act 1976 · CPD Bye-laws 2008 · PE = 5 yrs after RE + 17 CPD points + EPE · Washington Accord full member 2017 · safety of the public comes first.
Framework: PPRA Ordinance 2002 and Public Procurement Rules 2004 (federal); provinces have their own: Punjab PPRA Rules 2014, KPPRA Rules 2014, Sindh SPPRA Rules 2010, Balochistan BPPRA Rules 2014.
Response time (Rule 13): Not less than 15 days for national competitive bidding and 30 days for international competitive bidding, counted from first publication.
Advertisement: Above the threshold: PPRA website + newspapers (one English, one Urdu national daily); e-PADS for e-procurement.
Bid security: Not more than 5% of the estimated value (fixed amount, so as not to reveal the estimate).
Performance security: Commonly up to 10% of contract price, valid until completion/defects liability.
Bid validity extension: May be extended once, by not more than the original validity period; bidders refusing may withdraw without forfeiting bid security.
Repeat order: Not to exceed 15% of the original order value.
Bidding procedures: Single-stage one-envelope (simple works), single-stage two-envelope (technical + financial, opened separately), two-stage, two-stage two-envelope (complex/turnkey).
Evaluation: Lowest evaluated bid (not necessarily lowest price) is awarded; evaluation report published before award; grievance redressal committee for complaints.
PPRA: 15 days national / 30 days international; bid security ≤ 5%; repeat order ≤ 15%.
Forms: PC-I (project proposal/cost), PC-II (feasibility/survey), PC-III (progress monitoring), PC-IV (completion report), PC-V (annual operational report for 5 years after completion).
Fig. — Project cycle: PC-II → PC-I → approval forum → PSDP/ADP funding → PC-III → PC-IV → PC-V.
Budgets: PSDP — Public Sector Development Programme (federal); ADP — Annual Development Programme (provincial).

Note: Limits are revised from time to time (e.g., ECNEC threshold was Rs 3 bn → Rs 10 bn in 2020 → Rs 7.5 bn in 2022). Quote the latest notification in the exam.
PC-I = proposal, PC-II = feasibility, PC-III = monitoring, PC-IV = completion, PC-V = operation. ECNEC is the highest approval forum.

Sequence: Rough cost estimate → Administrative Approval (AA, by the administrative department/forum) → detailed estimate → Technical Sanction (TS, by the competent engineer — XEN/SE/CE by limit) → funds allocation → tender (NIT) → comparative statement → acceptance → work order/agreement → execution → measurement → bills → completion → final bill & completion certificate.

AA vs TS: AA = formal acceptance of the need and cost by the administrative authority; TS = engineer’s guarantee that the design and detailed estimate are sound and economical. No work starts without both and allotment of funds.

Rates: Punjab: Market Rate System (MRS) issued periodically by the Finance Department for each district (material, labour, hire charges) + Composite Schedule of Rates (CSR) analysed rates; KP and other provinces have their own schedules. Non-schedule items are rated by rate analysis.

Measurement Book (MB): Government record of every measurement — the basis of all payments; entries in ink, no erasures (cut and initial); measurements test-checked by SDO/XEN as per departmental rules.

Bills: Running (on-account) bill — interim payment for work measured so far, subject to final adjustment; final bill — after completion and final measurement. Deductions: income tax, sales tax, retention money/security, recovery of advances.

Advances: Mobilisation advance (against bank guarantee, recovered from running bills); secured advance on non-perishable materials brought to site (commonly up to 75% of their value), recovered as materials are used.
Estimate add-ons: Contingencies (≈ 3–5%) and work-charged establishment (≈ 1.5–2%) added to detailed estimates; revised estimate when sanctioned cost is to be exceeded beyond the permissible limit.

Contract terms: Liquidated damages for delay (capped, commonly ≈ 10% of contract price); defects liability / defects notification period (usually 12 months, FIDIC 365 days); price escalation clause for long contracts.
Registers: Material at site account, stock register, cement register, site order book (instructions to contractor), hindrance register (delays), daily diary.
Measurement Book is the basis of payment; running bill = on-account payment; Technical Sanction comes after Administrative Approval.
